The Gepids were a Germanic people closely related to the Goths who settled in the region of Pannonia and the Balkans, controlling key territorial passages in central Europe. Yet their independence was short-lived. Under Attila's dominion, they were conquered and held as tributaries of the Huns, forced to provide troops and acknowledge Hunnic overlordship. After the Hunnic empire collapsed in 453, the Gepids briefly regained independence and ruled a kingdom in Pannonia under kings like Ardaric. This respite lasted only decades. They were eventually defeated and destroyed by the Ostrogoths under Theodoric the Great in the 480s and 490s, losing their territorial independence entirely. After that defeat, the Gepids gradually disappeared from historical records as a distinct people, absorbed into the Ostrogothic kingdom and later into the successor Balkan peoples. They remain one of the lesser-known Germanic peoples, in part because their history was so heavily shaped by the more powerful forces around them—the Huns, the Ostrogoths, and later Byzantine expansion. Yet for a time, they controlled strategic Balkan and Pannonian territory that made them important to the military and political calculations of far larger powers.
